doc.title: Sonny Igoe interviewed by Monk Rowe, Emerson, New Jersey, July 31, 2003

title: Returning to Woody Herman after a failed studio try
summary: After one $12 Downbeat gig with Parker and Mingus, Igoe rejoins Herman for $150 and leaves his wife $1.19.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Yeah. Stick with being a Boy Scout. Well tell me a little about making a living in the studio scene in New York.

Well that was one of the happiest times in my life because I was always home and saw my children, and saw my children grow up. Because I missed so much of my first daughter when I was with Woody. He gave me time to go home for the baby and I had to quit to get the time. And so he had another two or three drummers. I was out of the band for ten weeks. And so our baby was now close to ten weeks old, okay? And I get a call, I thought that I already played with Woody Herman, I already played with Benny Goodman successfully, I should be able to make it in the New York recording scene. I’d just hang around and meet guys and get work. Failure. Complete failure. I worked one job in ten weeks. It paid twelve dollars. And on that job we had two bands. It was at a jazz club in New York called the Downbeat. And it was on 54th Street just off Eighth Avenue. And the first band was Charlie Parker, Max Roach, the bass player was Mingus, Charlie Mingus, and I forget who the piano player was. And we had two trombone players, Kai Winding and Bill Harris from my Woody Herman days, and the rhythm section, myself and Percy Heath was the bass player and I forget who the piano player was in it. Anyway we played, this was my first job in ten weeks. We played alternating sets from nine to four in the morning. That’s what we used to play, three or four, I forget which. But anyway, we all made the same: Charlie Parker, everybody. Twelve bucks. We all make twelve bucks. That was it. That was the only job I had. So I get a call from Woody’s manager and he says, “hey Sonny, Woody’s not that happy with anybody since you left,” he said, “would you consider coming back with the band?” And I said, “sure,” I said, “can I get a little bit more money?” He says, “yeah I think so,” he says, “how much more?” So now I’m thinking $125, right? So I said, “well how about $150 clear?” So he’d pay my taxes. He said, “yeah, we’ll do that.” But he didn’t do it.

But he gave me $150 clear but he didn’t pay any taxes. So anyway somehow or other he got away with it. But anyway I left home, right? The baby is now ten weeks old. So I’m getting the vast estate in order. I had rent was about 95 bucks and I had a 90 dollar a month car payment and I had a small insurance policy I was paying off. And so I did the

checkbook and I said, “okay hon, I’m leaving you with $119,” which is our entire estate. So she says, “that’s fine.” Because we didn’t worry about money back then. You know we were young, in love and a new baby and the hell with it. So anyway I went back with the band. I had to go to Pittsburgh. And I got off at Pittsburgh for the first job and I knew the hotel I was going to so there was a call waiting for me, and it was my wife saying, “are you there yet?” And I said, “well of course I’m here, what’s up?” She said, “well you made a terrible mistake, I had to call to tell you this.” And I said, “what do you mean I made a terrible mistake?” She said, “you didn’t leave me with $119, you left with $1.19.” And I said, “oh my God I’ll have to borrow some money from the manager and send you some money.” So I borrowed a hundred bucks and wired it to her. And that was the way that second career with Woody Herman started. In debt.
You had nowhere to go but up I guess.
